subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, May 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for the second reading of bill No. 91, respecting banks and banking, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Bill No. 91, an act respecting banks and banking, contains provisions which will govern the conditions of the extension of bank charters for the next ten years. It may well be said that economic conditions in Canada for the next ten years will be governed by this bill. For these and other reasons, I consider the bill to be of extreme importance. I regret to say, however, that to me the bill looks more like a charter for a new depression than a new lease on the economic life of the nation.
The stand of the Social Credit movement on monetary and economic matters should. I think, by this time be well known across this country. During the past nine years the Social Credit members of parliament havej placed upon the record of this house, time and again, some of the most enlightening material on the subject. The hon. members for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), Acadia (Mr. Quelch), and Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques), have

gained for themselves prominent recognition in this field. W'e may also include in this group three or four members from the Liberal ranks, the leading two of whom1 are the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) and the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght). Disappointing, however, is the fact that the Liberal monetary reformers talk monetary reform but always vote with, the government in support of reaction.
I would say that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) achieved the object which he aimed at by his speech of May 2. His twenty-one page provocation drew out the opposition groups to speak along the lines which he charted for them. This arrangement smothered a considerable amount of anticipated attack. As was said the other day, the minister took the offensive and in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the results so far show that he has had a measure of success.
The minister certainly showed courage when he undertook to divert the attention of the house from the inefficiency, shortcomings, and inadequacy of the government's policy, and to unleash a projected attack upon what he considered to be the unsound stand of apposition groups. In other words, the minister placed the opposition groups on trial before this house and the country, and he assumed the role of the prosecuting attorney. In my humble opinion the positions should have been reversed.
I should like to make only three or four references to the minister's speech of May 2. In the first place, the minister unloaded the blame for the last man-made depression on the first world war. No doubt his successors, by the same process of reasoning, will blame the next depression on the present war. In the second place, the minister quoted Professors Thorp and Mitchell as his authorities for Canada enjoying 1-86 years of prosperity for each year of depression. I am prepared to take the minister's word for the correctness of this statement. But would the minister mind explaining to the house and to the country why a nation as rich as Canada is should have one year of depression for every 1-86 years of prosperity? Why should there ever be depression in the midst of plenty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
May I say a word at this stage about that? The professors who made the study had the years divided into years of prosperity, revival, recession and depression, which were defined in accordance with their own principles. When that fact is taken into consideration the picture is certainly different from the impression given by me. Moreover, the period covered was from 1888 to 1924, and wras before the establishment of

Bank Act-Mr. Hlynka
many central banks, and certainly long before the time when central banks had developed and perfected techniques for controlling savings from prosperity to depression. But it must be admitted that in the period between 188S and 1924 there were business cycles. The point of the quotation was, of course, to show that Canada's position was better in that respect than that of all other countries or at least seventeen other countries.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
An argument to the effect that Canada has had more prosperity in decimal points than some of the other countries in the world does not prove to me that we should have any depression. Of course, if we think along the lines of reaction it. would seem to indicate that for this nation to enjoy 1-86 years of prosperity as against one year of depression is quite an achievement. But, as I said, the situation is one that cannot be justified.
The third point that I wish to refer to in the minister's speech is to me a significant statement which appears at page 2549 of Hansard of May 2. In defence of the government's policy the minister states:
There is no reason why the government should seek to escape the cost of interest on its borrowings at the expense of any one or all of these particular groups associated with the banks. The only equitable policy is for the government to pay reasonable rates of interest appropriate to the form and nature of the borrowing and meet the cost from taxation levied by parliament.
I believe that the shoe should be on the other foot. The minister says "Why should the government seek to escape the cost of interest on its borrowings at the expense of any one of those particular groups associated with the banks?" May I ask the minister this question: Why should the banks escape with the privilege of the issuing and withdrawing of credit which rightly belongs to the people? The minister further explains that he finds four objections to the social credit proposals, and they appear in Hansard to this effect: (1) That if the Social Crediters had their way the shareholders of the banks would have to suffer losses; that is, if the right to expand credit were restored to the people; (2) That the depositors would pay higher service charges; (3) That interest rates would have to be reduced on savings to depositors and, (4) that bank employees would get less in wages and salaries. May I state frankly that the four arguments advanced by the minister cannot hold water. Just as the inflation bogey became worn-out, threadbare, until the minister was forced to give up that argument, so will these four gems of wisdom eventually fall by the wayside.
The minister built up his wdiole argument on the premise that there was little wrong with the government's policy. However, he failed to explain to the house and to the country why the old status quo policy has failed so miserably in the past. Instead of devoting so much time to suppositions why the new proposals of opposition groups would not work, the minister would have rendered a service to the country had he confined himself to an explanation of how his policy will be made to work. This is one question, among others, that should have been answered by the minister. However, he sidestepped many important questions, and went on to build up his case against the new proposals. For this reason I desire to ask the minister a few questions, to which I should like categorical answers.
1.	Would the minister tell this house and the country by what method he intends to repay the staggering debt of this dominion? Does he consider it necessary to repay it and, if so, when does he intend to begin?
2.	Would he tell us how he proposes to meet the interest falling due each year on our huge national debt? Is he aware of the fact that 44-04 per cent of our national income in 1934 was swallowed up by interest charges on our national debt, leaving only 55-96 per cent of the national income to take care of all other expenses? That was the situation when our national debt was only 83,141,042,097. What will be the situation when our national debt reaches the fifteen billion dollar mark after the war?
3.	Will the minister give us the assurance that no money consideration will be permitted to stand in the way of our post-war reconstruction? He did give us this assurance as far as the prosecution of the war was concerned. Will he now give us the same assurance in respect to the peace-time requirements of this nation? I feel that the people of Canada should have this question answered.
4.	The minister did not explain by what manner of means he intends to place sufficient purchasing power in the hands of the people of Canada to enable them to buy the goods and services they require to maintain a decent standard of living. This standard of living should be commensurate with the wealth of this nation, which we can give our people in goods and services.
I will make this statement, that if the government continues to pursue its present financial policy it will put an end to private enterprise in Canada. Socialist critics at the present time are using the argument that private enterprise is to be blamed for the many ills from which the people of Canada
Bank Act-Mr. Hlynka

have suffered in the past, and I can tell the government that there seems to be a considerable number of willing listeners to that unsound argument. These critics refuse to admit that it was the monetary system which failed to distribute the goods that private enterprise was ready to produce. I believe in private enterprise for the farmer, for the business man and in other pursuits, but I wish to make it clear that I oppose any and all monopolies, government or private. It is my considered opinion that all economic reform is based on monetary reform; and unless the government is ready and willing to give the Canadian people real monetary reform, all talk of reconstruction, housing schemes, rehabilitation schemes, old age pension schemes, health schemes, educational schemes, a floor under the income of the farmer and so on will remain idle and futile, in the words of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).
Social Crediters have two main slogans which I believe express at least in part the social credit philosophy. The first is: "What is physically possible must be made financially possible." May I illustrate the point? If in time of war we had men and material, would we refuse to manufacture the weapons of war because there was no money? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that no government would dare advance this "no money" argument in time of war so long as men and materials were available. That has been amply proven during this war. Now let us take a peace-time period. If we have materials which the people need, shall we continue to tell them that we cannot feed and clothe them because there is no money? Any government permitting such a condition to exist after the war will have no place in Canada. Our second slogan is: "Security with freedom." Not only do we propose to give our people .security; we will assist them in guarding jealously the hard-won freedoms for which [DOT]our forefathers laid down their lives. At the present time we hear men prominent in our public life stressing in their speeches and in written articles the material and economic :side of life. I agree that the economic side [DOT]of life is most important. I agree that the people of this rich nation no longer should tolerate anything which would resemble the pre-war years. 1 believe the Canadian people should be enjoying the highest possible standard of living. At the same time, to become purely materialistic, we hear theories advanced along these lines: promises made to the people that all they have to do is give up part of their freedom, give their consent to certain amounts of regimentation, and they
(Mr. Hlynka.]
will be guaranteed security. I feel that the time has come when hon. members should rise and declare their stand on this important point. We must draw a distinct line between those proposals which would land us eventually in a totalitarian set-up, and those which would guarantee the people national economic security and freedom.
Therefore I repeat that the Social Crediters have two main slogans. The first is: "What is physically possible must be made financially possible," and the second: "Security with freedom."
If this bank bill is the best the minister and the government can produce then I personally feel that the people of this nation will demand that the minister and the government guarantee to them the results which they want and the things which they need. As I pointed out, 55-96 per cent of our total national income in 1934 was left to discharge our obligations, to pay old age pensions, to pay our civil servants and to take care of all other expenses that enter into government. Our national debt has now risen until it is in the neighbourhood of S15 billion. I say then that the people of this country cannot expect any improvement along economic lines unless our money system is changed. I for one am disappointed to find that the best the government can do, after the heroic achievements of the men and women in our armed forces, is to bring down a bill which, as I said, reads more like a death warrant than a new lease on the economic life of this nation.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the first member supporting the government to speak this afternoon I should like to express our pride and gratification at the eloquent, moving and statesmanlike speech of the leader of this house, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King), before both houses of parliament in London this morning. I feel that it was a most historic occasion, and the speech of the Prime Minister was worthy of the great occasion and our great country which he so ably represents at the present time.
At the outset of my remarks I wish to commend the Minister of Finance for the able and thoughtful speech he made when he introduced this bill with respect to banks and banking. It was alleged to be provocative, but the thought occurred . to me that surely the minister had the right to defend the system of regulated free enterprise in which he believes, just as anyone else has the right to attack that system. It seems to me that there has been growing up in the country on the part

Bank Act-Mr. Tucker
of some people a strategy of making violent attacks on the honesty of purpose and the integrity of motive of other parties. Then when those parties defend themselves, the parties who had made the first attack play the martyr and pretend that the others are the aggressors. It reminds me of the strategy which was employed recently by a certain man in European affairs. It enabled him to gain certain initial successes, but they are not remaining very permanent.
I commend the minister particularly for the information he gave in regard to the operations of the chartered banks. In qrder properly to understand and deal with these matters of laws regarding banking we must have this sort of information. The giving of such information recognized that these banks are administering a valuable franchise granted to them by this parliament on behalf of the people of Canada-and the people of Canada have a right to know how and in what manner they, the banks, are discharging the obligations which were placed upon them by the granting of this franchise.
This bill will renew the charters of ten banks for the period from 1944 to 1954. The decision we shall make and the bank charters which we shall establish will be, in my opinion, one of the most important pieces of legislation passed in this parliament. We shall be legislating for a decade which should see us win final victory over the aggressor nations of the world. That decade should see the return to this country of our gallant men and women of the armed services and their reestablishment in the civil life of the country. It should see, we hope, a period of the greatest prosperity that Canada has ever known. Most economists believe that such a post-war era of prosperity is possible if certain basic and now admittedly essential steps are taken.
The primary step which most economists seem to agree will have to be taken is to permit the free flow of international trade in this post-war era. Anyone who has studied the causes of the depression which started in 1931 will, I think, admit that the main cause, not only in the case of Canada but throughout the world, was the loss of export markets. This was owing to the chaotic conditions in Europe and the trade restrictions and other interferences with trade imposed by European nations in an attempt to prepare themselves for war if it should come.
Then in the ease of Canada there was an additional reason in that there was a period of almost ten years of most extensive and almost continuous crop failure in western Canada. This period extended from 1930 to 1938 inclusive. An attempt has been made to
attribute the ills from which Canada suffered during that period to our present economic system, but I feel that the majority of our people, after they study the facts which have been and will be laid before them, will reject decisively this attempt to mislead them. All countries experienced a depression during that period. In one socialist country which suffered no crop failures such as we had in Canada millions died of starvation during that period.
In this connection I should like to quote a well know western editor, I believe now deceased, Mr. Charles W. Peterson. He was editor of the Farm and Ranch Review of Calgary from 1912 on. In an article published not long before his death he said:
I have never been able to see how socialism would help the farmer in any substantial way. The crisis of the 1930's which is solely responsible for the existing political revolt on the prairies had nothing whatever to do with our "free enterprise" economy. We had a series of crop failures in the west which no political action could have prevented. And we had almost complete demoralization of prices solely due to conditions in Europe. The only useful thing any Canadian government-socialist or capitalist-could do was to help the fanner by way of public subsidies and relief, which, as we all knowr, was promptly done. Whether we had had Liberal Prime Minister King or High Commissar "Comrade" King, in command, the situation would have been neither better nor worse.
In approaching the revision of our banking system there seemed to be two points of view among the parties in Canada. I am not quite so sure about the present attitude of the Labour Progressive party, but leaving them out of the picture we have the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation advocating a gigantic state owned and operated banking monopoly. All other parties, as I understand their present attitude, wish to retain our present competitive banking system and to reform it in a greater or lesser degree.
I suggest that the purpose of a banking system should be to provide credit to a people, individually and collectively, to the extent that is in the best interests of this country, that it should be supplied as cheaply as possible, and without taking away the fundamental rights of the people.
In what way will a state-owned monopoly do this better than our present system? In the first place, will more credit be provided? Apparently the banks have taken more chances in regard to lending money than I had thought they had, until I heard the figures given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). According to those figures the average losses during the past fifteen years and up to and including 1942, less recoveries, averaged $13,800,000 a year. A more generous lending policy obviously
Bank Act-Mr. Tucker

would have entailed heavier losses and increased the cost of credit. One of the things that the advocates of socialist operation of banks would have to answer is this: Would a bank operated by government employees be more ready to take chances on sustaining losses than operators of private enterprise, who might be induced to take a chance in order to gain some profit? My experience of those in government positions is that they will not take chances because they have nothing to gain if it works out right and they have everything to lose if it works out wrong. So that I think the chances of getting a freer credit policy from a state-operated banking system would not be great.
Second, would it lead to cheaper credit? Institutions run in competition with one another are likely to be more efficient than any giant monopoly. This is even admitted by the leader of the C.C.F. party himself, when he says that if he took over the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, as he says he would do, he would operate it in competition with the Canadian National Railway. If it is a good thing to keep the two railway systems operating in competition with each other, why in the world would it not be a good thing to keep the banks operating in competition with one another? The answer of the C.C.F. is that they would create one state-owned banking monopoly.
It may be argued that a state-owned bank would operate at lower rates because it would not need to operate at a profit. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, from what I have seen of state-operated institutions, that the chances are that if they charged the same rates as the present banking institutions do they would probably have no profit. But, as it is, we do tax that profit at a heavy rate and leave only enough to give a reasonable return on the capital invested, plus compensation for risks run and efficient management, plus a certain amount to cover possible losses in the years which might not be so prosperous.
It may be that the banks, on the basis of present interest rates, are making a higher profit than they perhaps should. The answer to that is that the rates have been coming down ever since this government came into office in 1935, and I feel that that process should be continued. You do not have to socialize the banks in order to reduce bank profits to a fair level.
There is, however, an overriding consideration which I think at this time is most important, particularly now when we are spending the precious lives of our sons to protect our democratic and free institutions.

I submit that the more you extend the field of government action, the more you endanger our present democratic system. When everyone is working for the government, the government becomes master of the people and the people become servants of the state. Indeed this is the avowed purpose of the leader of the C.C.F. party and of the C.C.F. in socializing the banks. To prove that, I should like to read from an article by the leader of the C.C.F. party which appeared in Maclean's magazine of September 1, 1943. Here is what he said:
However, there are certain key industries control of which automatically brings about control over the economy as a whole. The financial machinery, transportation, electric power and large monopolies are such key industries.
Then in the C.C.F. book, "Make this Your Canada", written by David Lewis, national secretary of the C.C.F. party, and Frank Scott, national chairman of the C.C.F., with a foreword by M. J. Coldwell, national president of the C.C.F. and member for Rosetown-Biggar in this house, which publication was issued August 16, 1943, the Regina manifesto of the C.C.F. party is given, and I quote the second plank, in part:
Socialization of Finance.
Socialization of all financial machinery- banking, currency, credit, and insurance, to make possible the effective control of currency, credit and prices, and the supplying of new productive equipment for socially desirable purposes.
Planning by itself will be of little use if the public authority has not the power to carry its plans into effect. Such power will require the control of finance and of all those vital industries and services, which, if they remain in private hands, can be used to thwart or corrupt the will of the public authority. Control of finance is the first step to the control of the whole economy.
I emphasize the last sentence:
Control of finance is the first step to the control of the whole economy.
It goes on to say what their ultimate objective is:
No C.C.F. government will rest content until it has eradicated capitalism and put into operation the full programme of socialized planning which will lead to the establishment in Canada of the cooperative common-wealth.
It might be objected that the present C.C.F. does not adhere to that manifesto; but the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well), writing in Maclean's magazine of September 1, 1943, said this:
Question (1) is wrong in seeming to assume that there has been any confusion between the original Regina manifesto and any later pronouncements either by myself or by the party as a whole. The manifesto was and remains a statement of the basic principles of the C.C.F.

Bank Act-Mr. Tucker
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), speaking in this house the other day, said, as reported at page 2731 of Hansard:
I say to the minister that we do not believe in socializing anything just for the fun of socializing it.
The pronouncements of the Regina manifesto on behalf of the president and the secretary of the C.C.F. party, endorsed by the leader of the party, are more authoritative on that point than any pronouncement by the hon. member for Weyburn. I submit that the hon. member for Weyburn should not in this house or in the country pretend that their policy is not socialization when it is the admitted policy of their party. He went on to say, still on page 2731 of Hansard:
There can be only one criterion as to whether or not anything should be operated by the public, and that is whether it can thereby be operated to the better advantage of the community as a whole than by leaving it in private hands.
There is another criterion and it is a more important criterion still. Admittedly at times a benevolent autocrat might operate our state more efficiently for a period of time than we can under our democratic system. But is this all we care about in this country of ours? Is our democratic, system worth so little that we would barter it away in order to get a benevolent autocracy that might be able to administer the country more efficiently for a time than our democratic system? Are we to sacrifice our freedom and political democracy for an alleged improvement in our economic lot? I say "alleged," because it is the history of mankind that after peoples have placed themselves in the hands of an all-wise dictator they generally find that he ultimately makes a big mistake which does more harm in one year than he has done of good in all the previous years of his government, and if he manages not to make a mistake he is invariably followed by somebody who does. In other words, Caesar Augustus was followed by Nero.
The danger is great. So-called democratic socialism of the sweeping type advocated by the C.C.F. is bound, in my opinion, to lead to dictatorship in the long run, and maybe not so long either.
The Liberal party favoured the Bank of Canada as a nationally owned1 and controlled institution, and brought it into existence as such, because it was deemed that on balance it was in the best interest of the people to bring it under government ownership and control and that by doing so there was no great threat to the democratic liberties of the people of Canada as a whole. I submit that, if ever the question arises, if it could be shown that
monopolistic government banking would operate somewhat more cheaply, if it would endanger the fundamental democratic liberties of our people, we would not want it. We want no dictator in Canada, no matter how smart he may be, no matter how wonderful the promises he makes of how much better off we shall be if we place ourselves within his power.
Therefore I believe the present competitive and controlled commercial banking system is better than the gigantic monopolistic banking system proposed by the C.C.F. I know it can be improved so as to serve the people better than any state-owned monopoly could or would, and since the object and result of government ownership and control of the whole banking system by any party is admittedly the dictatorial control of our nation, I shall oppose the amendment.
I stated at the outset that all other parties than the C.C.F. believe in improving our present banking system. I believe.our party has accomplished real reforms in the years it has been in power. The first great reform was to establish full ownership and control of the Bank of Canada by the people of Canada as represented by this government and this parliament. Anyone who understands the nature of the powers of the Bank of Canada realizes that the government, by being in control of it, in the last analysis has absolute control of the issue of currency and credit in this country, as to the volume to be issued, not of course as to who individually shall receive it.
What has been the record since control has been taken by the Bank of Canada of the financial system of this country? I should like to give the house figures indicating the decrease in the cost of money to our government since 1936.
On March 31, 1935 the average rate of interest paid on direct governmental borrowing was 4T5 per cent. If you take into account the $14 millions which was returned by the Bank of Canada to the consolidated fund, the net cost-the interest on-our governmental borrowing had been reduced to 2-45 per cent per annum on December 31, 1943. On March 31, 1935, it was 4-15 per cent per annum; on December 31, 1943 it was 2-45 per cent per annum. That is a reduction of 1-70 per cent per annum in that period of time, a reduction of over 40 per cent in the interest rate paid by our government on its direct borrowings. That was achieved in a period of nine years, and if the same rate of reduction were maintained in the next ten years the rate would actually be cut down to T7 per cent per annum, or $17 interest for the use of $10,000 for one year. This indicates the rapid progress
Bank Act-Mr. Tucker

which has been made in reducing the interest burden of our borrowings since the central bank was placed in charge of our financial system. As far as I am concerned I am favourable to continuing the present process of reducing the cost of governmental borrowings to a point where it will amount to only a small service charge. I am convinced that if we are to carry out the great reform programme which we intend to carry out and maintain a programme of full employment, we shall have to get the cost of governmental borrowing down to a level where it will represent only a small service charge, and we have been proceeding in that direction very rapidly. I earnestly commend the government for the progress it has made in that direction.
One of the means by which the Bank of Canada has effected this result is by the heavy purchase of government bonds and securities. Since March 31, 1935, it has increased its holdings of government bonds and securities from $152,100,000 to $1,345,900,000, an increase of $1,193,800,000. This credit costs the government nothing except the extra cost of operating the Bank of Canada in consequence of the purchase of these securities, because the income made by collecting the interest on them is turned over to the consolidated fund, less cost of operation. These operations have another and most important effect: they load the banks up with cash reserves on which th y must pay interest to depositors, and since, according to the figures given by the Minister of Finance, the average rate of interest on all bank deposits was -53 per cent per annum, if all that billion dollars were taken by the people who received it and deposited in the banks, it would lead to an extra cost in interest to the chartered banks of this country of $5,300,000 per annum. This, I think, accounts for the willingness of the banks to buy short-term treasury bills. If they cannot loan their credit to private enterprise, rather than have it lie idle they must find some means of using it, and the system of treasury bills and deposit certificates has been resorted to. It is interesting to compare what we pay in interest to the banks of this country for these short-term loans with what the United States and Great Britain pay. On the last issue of treasury bills we pay -387 per cent per annum. Concurrently the United States is paying -375 per cent, almost the same, while the United Kingdom pays -999 per cent, over twice as much. As of December 31, 1943, there were over one billion dollars of treasury bills and deposit certificates outstanding. This substantial item indicates that almost all the extra money 
issued by the Bank of Canada has had to be reinvested by the banks and financial institutions in these low interest-bearing treasury bills, on which the last rate of interest was -387 per cent per annum, and the highest rate paid since March 31, 1943, was -498 per cent per annum, less than one-half of one per cent per annum.
Naturally, the banks would gladly lend at higher rates of interest if they could find borrowers, but the farmers of the country, for example, are paying off their loans as rapidly as possible. The figures in this regard are quite interesting. Bank loans on October 31, 1939, as compared with October 31, 1943 were: Farmers loans, cattle and fruitraisers' loans, October 31, 1939, $57,000,000, and in 1943. $49,800,000, a reduction of $7,000,000. Manufacturers' loans, however, owing, I suppose, to the war, increased from $192,600,000 on October 31, 1939, to $302,800,000 on October 31, 1943. Naturally, after the war there will be great expansion of industries to produce civilian goods, and the banks will be anxious to lend as much money as possible at a higher rate of interest than less than one-half of one per cent per annum. This will be particularly true of loans of intermediate credit under the proposed agricultural improvement act, because those loans will be in effect guaranteed by the government. I understand that an aggregate amount of 10 per cent of loans will be guaranteed.
That brings up a point which I wish to press on the attention of the minister. I feel under these circumstances that these loans should bear a top rate interest of 3 per cent per annum, and I say so for this reason. The cost of money to the banks, according to the figures given by the minister, which includes cost of paying interest on deposits, remuneration of employees, provision for taxes, contribution to pension fund, depreciation of bank premises, and all other current operating expenses, is 2-28 per cent of their total assets for the year 1943. The average total operating earnings are 2-86 per cent of total assets. If the average total earnings of the banks is 2-86 per cent, I submit that this money, used to assist farmers in getting labour-saving machinery and in building better homes for themselves, should be given to them at approximately the average rate of the bank's income. In other words, I suggest 3 per cent, and since their average cost of operation is 2-28 per cent of their assets, on these loans, which in effect are government-guaranteed, they would still be making, roughly -75 per cent per annum, or more than their average rate of profit.

Bank Act-Mr. Tucker
It is important that the farmers be given this consideration, because of their past difficulties and the present great contribution they are making to our war effort. Many of them are working long past the age at which they should be working. They are making a really tremendous contribution to the war effort of Canada, and they should therefore, in my opinion, receive special consideration after the war in order that they may obtain labour-saving machinery as soon as possible and be in a position to build for themselves homes with modern conveniences just as good as those which the people in the cities have. The government, I repeat, in making loans available at 3 per cent will not be putting a burden on the banks, because the banks are actually making on their assets an average of less than 3 per cent per annum.
That raises another point, namely, the top limit of interest on ordinary loans. I submit that the top limit should be five per cent and not six per cent as proposed in this bill. At the time when the government was borrowing money on long-term bonds at 5i per cent, the top rate of legal interest chargeable by the banks was seven per cent. Now we are paying only three per cent on long-term loans. We have reduced the interest paid by the government on long-term loans by 2J per cent, and I submit that we should reduce the top rate of interest chargeable on private loans by at least two per cent, making five per cent, the legal rate of interest in this country, the limit which banks can charge.
Undoubtedly competition will tend to reduce the rate of interest, but it does not operate so much in favour of the small borrower as it does in favour of the large borrower. It was found in recent years that the banks were charging six per cent in city districts and particularly in Ontario, while they were still charging seven per cent in western Canada and in the maritimes. A top rate of interest would protect the little man who is not able to bargain. The big man can bargain and get a rate of five per cent or less, but if you have a top rate fixed you protect the little man, because he is generally charged the legal limit. I would ask the minister to consider this proposal very seriously.
I am told that the banks, some of them anyway, have followed the policy of refusing to do business with anyone who has taken advantage of an act passed by this parliament, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. If that is true; if they have taken that attitude, then they are in effect defying this parliament, because parliament put that act on the statute books for the benefit of the farmers so that
they might avail themselves of it; and if the bankers, the people who administer public credit, are doing something they should not do-

speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman quite right about the act to which he refers?

speechtext: The hon. gentleman said the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
I meant the Farmers'
Creditors Arrangement Act. The bankers are administering a public utility, and they should be responsible to some public authority for the manner in which that administration is carried on. If there are such cases or others there should be someone to whom an aggrieved person could appeal and who could look into the matter, and his report, together with the protest, should be submitted to the government and parliament and be subject to investigation, if deemed proper, by the banking and commerce committee or some other public authority. The banks should be made to feel that they have not absolute authority as to persons to whom they may give credit and those from whom they may withhold it, without perhaps being answerable to parliament for any arbitrary act.
The railways cannot close agencies without getting the permission of the board of transport commissioners, and I submit that the banks should not be permitted to curtail the services which they give the people without the permission of some public authority. In all these matters we should bring the banks under more direct control. One of my hon. friends of the Conservative party just now suggested in a very-well, I would not say he sneered, but he said "Wouldn't that be wonderful?" I submit that the banks must be made to realize that they are administering a public utility and are answerable to parliament for how they do it.
Another feature of this government's programme for which I should like to commend them is the foreign exchange control board.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext: My hon. friend referred to someone in our party having said something.

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext: I did not like to name him. I see him sitting here.

speechtext: Is it on Hansard?

subtopic: CONDITIONS GOVERNING TEN-YEAR EXTENSION OF BANK CHARTERS
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is on Hansard or not. I heard it. It does not have to be on Hansard. If they do not want me to refer to it, do not let them say it behind my back. I do not blame the leader
2S18
Bank Act-Mr. Tucker

of the opposition for not wanting that to appear in Hansard as coming from one of his own party.
I was referring to the foreign exchange control board. This should be continued to the extent necessary to prevent in the future such things happening as have occurred in the past. We have seen instances where men have made large fortunes from developing the mining resources of the country and have then removed those fortunes from Canada. We have also seen cases where manufacturers have made large fortunes under the protection of our tariff policy, and then have taken that money to other countries, sometimes to countries where they pay lower labour rates, to set up industries in competition with the industries which they have asked to have protected in this country.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that we must have some form of control so that sort of thing does not happen in the future, and wealth that is built up out of the resources of this country and by virtue of the protection enjoyed under the laws of this country should be kept here in order that it may be subject to our income taxes and our succession duty taxes.
In closing, may I say that when this bill as amended becomes law it will confer a valuable franchise on the banks. It will be giving them the right as trustees to handle a large share of the credit of this country. That trusteeship has been very carefully adhered to in so far as their obligation to their depositors is concerned; but their attitude toward the people of western Canada during the period of 1930 to 1939 makes me feel that it must be brought home to the banks that in handling that great franchise they are not absolute masters, but are answerable to this parliament and to the people of Canada. They must be made to feel that they must handle it in accordance with the best interests of this country. In order to bring that home to them I think some public authority should be established to which they must be answerable and which will then make a report in proper cases to this parliament.
As I said before, this bill is one by which we are legislating for a period of ten years. During that time our troops will return from overseas where they have been defending our country and defending our system of freedom and democracy. One of the things they say over and over again is: "We do not want to return to things as they were from 1930 to 1939"-to depression and unemployment. I am glad this government at this crucial time takes the attitude, as I understand it does in the speech from the throne, that regardless of

what happens with respect to matters beyond our control in the way of foreign trade and so on, it will see to it that conditions are not permitted to get in the state they were in from 1930 to 1939-that the individual is ensured real security. I think the government's programme, including such things as a floor on farm prices, family allowances, reduction of interest rates and the other controls that it is setting up, including the farm improvement loan bill and other companion measures that the government has put into effect or will put into effect this session, will introduce such a measure of reform and social security that Canada will, after this war, enter a period of the greatest happiness and prosperity that this country has ever seen.
Mr. II. R. JACKMAN (Rosedale): Bill No. 91 does not call for any lengthy remarks on my part at the present time. On the whole I believe the amendments should be salutary and lead to greater satisfaction of the credit needs of our community. We look forward to the introduction of the farm improvement loan bill to see what further provisions are provided therein, and it is our fervent desire that every possible credit facility be afforded to the farming and fishing industries of this country.
May I say here, however, Mr. Speaker, that the spirit in which those provisions are administered means almost as much as does the actual wording of the provisions themselves. We shall look forward to the particular set-up of the farm improvement loan bill to see exactly what the provisions are before we are able to pass judgment. As it is, the amendments carried out in Bill No. 91, substituting the new Bank Act for the old. do make more forms of agricultural property available for the extension of credit by the banks than heretofore, and to that extent the new bill is an improvement. While it may not be entirely within the province of this parliament, nevertheless I believe that the chartered banks should so further the intention of the provisions which are passed by this house that they will endeavour to make their branch managers not merely judges of the credit worthiness of those who apply for loans, but also salesmen of credit, so that where there is a good business man or a good farmer who can use additional credit usefully and economically the bank manager will not necessarily sit back in his office and wait until he is approached, but will be encouraged and trained by the banks themselves to go out and put the credit to effective use. In that way our whole business and agricultural activity will be greatly stimulated.

Bank Act-Mr. Jackman
I am told by those who have had longer experience than I that there was a time in the development of this country when the bank managers actively sought to get their credits out; but that has to a large extent ceased during the last two or three decades.
I should also like to point out a word of ^caution to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) in regard to the provisions affecting the small personal loans. If those personal loans are to be extended as far as granting credit by the chartered banks is concerned, it might be that the better ones, the so-called cream of the small loans, will flow to the chartered banks, leaving only the more risky, more troublesome and more costly ones to the ordinary finance companies; with the result that the personal finance companies, which are to-day functioning, might find they *will have to refuse the service to necessitous borrowers, a service which they have provided for in emergencies; or the personal finance companies will have to ask to have the rates which they charge at the present time raised. Those rates, as we all know, are regarded by many as extremely high, although they may not result in any undue profits to the companies themselves.
Then again, the minister has said that he would welcome recommendations by the committee on banking and commerce on several specific matters. May I say, however, that this is not the first time he has suggested that the banking and commerce committee make a recommendation to this house and to himself. The last time the recommendations were made

which I may say did carry by a narrow majority-they were simply flouted when they came to the house, and the minister went on his own way and paid little or no heed to the resolution passed by the banking and commerce committee. It is no wonder that in such circumstances the minister deservedly finds attached to himself such words as "stubborn and narrow"; and there is a feeling on the part of a large body of the house that it is not the will of the people's representatives that is carried out in many of the financial measures but rather the will of certain people who are in the confidence of and who advise the minister.

I would point out, however, that the industrial development bank is not likely to have a great number of customers. It may have a thousand industrial customers, whereas the commercial banks have probably well over a million customers who are also voters. Nevertheless the principle is the same. Once the government gets into the banking business it gets into the business of securing votes willy-nilly and to some extent, perhaps a large extent under certain circumstances, it will find that political pressure is brought to bear, and that banking cannot be carried on free of political influence as long as it is under government administration. With the central bank, the Bank of Canada, the situation is vastly different, because that bank does not deal with the public directly and, therefore, is not concerned with and cannot influence votes one way or the other. I should like to point out that under Sir Adam Beck the Ontario hydro electric system for many years was entirely free of political influence, but after the last Liberal regime in Ontario came into power there came a time when the Ontario hydro electric system became the football of politics.

If the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) wishes to justify his remarks he is entitled to do so at some other time, but for the present I challenge his statement.
Therefore the industrial development bank, like the Ontario hydro electric commission, may very well find itself perfectly safe and free from politics for a number of years; yet almost inevitably there comes a time when the
Bank Act-Mr. Jackman

most vital force in our community, namely the political force and the attainment of power, overrides all other considerations. What was the situation in Ontario? For a very short time during the depression we had a temporary excess of power, and the contracts we had with Quebec power companies were cancelled by the then premier and the then attorney general, now the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck). If these contracts had not been made originally; if the power companies had not been developed to the extent they were, our present war effort would have been greatly handicapped. So that it is not only likely but inevitable in connection with some of these public institutions which should be maintained under a private system-true, under government regulation where necessary -that when they come under government administration temporary political considerations will outweigh economic planning which is designed only to serve the people and not to wrest power for some political purpose.
So much for political influences. One fears for the life of this industrial development bank because it is so entirely under the control of the government. But just as the government cannot argue both ways, so the C.C.F. cannot argue that the financial system of this country- has battened on its ill-gotten gains- which I do not admit for one moment-and at the same time argue, like the devil citing scripture for his own purposes, that the financial system is no good because in a time of stress the government had to give it assistance. The leader of the C.C.F. made much of the order in council which was passed during the depths of the depression and which established conventional values for certain securities held by some of our large institutions. The purpose of this order in council was, of course, that public confidence should not be lost; and these conventional values which were established, at a level somewhat higher than market values, were more representative of the inherent value of the securities themselves than were the market prices, which were merely the prices in the open market at a particular time. It is very much the same as wheat selling at forty cents, when every hon. member knows that is by no means a fair price for that commodity and does not represent the inherent value of it. As was pointed out in the house the other day, the government also had to come to the assistance of the wheat pools because the initial payment was larger than the price to which wheat subsequently fell. I was amused to hear the statement made that the bankers had wrongly advised the heads of the cooperative pools by telling them to make a larger initial payment than
fMr. Jackman.]
they should have made, and that when the market fell below the amount of the initial payments the bankers drove a hard bargain. ,1 can scarcely imagine that any member of the C.C.F. party would have advised a smaller initial payment than that which was made and which was recommended by the chartered banks, according to what I have heard.
The C.C.F. cannot at one and the same time say that the financial system is an octopus which feeds gluttonously, and then say it is so weak that it needs a blood transfusion. The only purpose of the order in council establishing conventional values was to endeavour to reestablish confidence on the part of the people; and the fact that the order in council was needed merely goes to show that finance suffered during the depression just as much as did business or labour. It has been pointed out also that the people who make up the financial community are drawn from all classes in this country, the same as with most other occupations, and that they are motivated by the same reasons. Indeed I have found little difference in human nature wherever I have come in contact with it. Everywhere there are good and bad; everyone must be responsible to some higher authority, just as parliament must be responsible to the people. I believe I heard the leader of the C.C.F. party quote Lord Acton in these words:
All power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely.
The banking system is not only responsible to parliament; it is responsible also to relentless and inexorable economic laws.
